_note: Insurance accounting standards & FSLI-level GAAP-vs-STAT explainers. Each article ships sections, fsli_table, references, last_updated. Every field is search-indexed.

articles.title: Cash & Cash Equivalents
articles.summary: Cash on hand, demand deposits, and short-term highly-liquid instruments with original maturities of 90 days or less. Identical concept under GAAP and STAT, but admissibility rules diverge sharply.
articles.key_difference: STAT non-admits restricted, foreign-bank, and concentration-excess cash. GAAP recognizes everything but discloses restrictions.
articles.gaap_view: Recognized at face value; restricted balances disclosed separately. Money-market funds with redemption-on-demand qualify as cash equivalents.
articles.stat_view: Reported on Schedule E Part 1 (cash) and Part 2 (cash equivalents). Non-admitted if held in unauthorized banks, restricted/escrow, or in excess of FDIC concentration limits.
articles.body_md:
## What it is

Cash & cash equivalents represent the most liquid asset class on an insurer's balance sheet. The line includes:

- Demand deposits at banks
- Petty cash and undeposited receipts
- Money-market mutual funds (Class 1 NAIC)
- Treasury bills with original maturity ≤ 90 days
- Repurchase agreements with maturity ≤ 90 days
- Commercial paper (top-tier, ≤ 90-day maturity)

## Why insurers care

Cash is the immediate-loss-paying asset. Property-cat insurers stress-test liquidity assuming a 1-in-100-year event drains the operating account in 5–10 days.

## Admissibility under SAP

Non-admitted cash reduces statutory surplus dollar-for-dollar. Statutory accounting disallows: cash in non-licensed foreign banks, restricted balances, bank balances exceeding FDIC limits at non-A-rated institutions.

sections.heading: Recognition
sections.content: Recognize when the insurer obtains the right to use the funds. Demand deposits → on settlement; cash equivalents → on trade date.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
items: Treating 6-month CDs as cash equivalents (wrong — that's a short-term investment).
Ignoring restricted cash (must be disclosed and may be non-admitted under STAT).
Excluding bank overdrafts from operating cash flows.

fsli_table.stat: Admitted at face if at authorized US banks
Admitted; NAV from Schedule D Pt 2

fsli_table.stat: Schedule DA Pt 1; admitted lower of cost or FV

articles.title: Bonds & Mortgage-Backed Securities
articles.summary: Largest asset class for most insurers (60–80% of invested assets). GAAP classifies as HTM/AFS/Trading; STAT carries NAIC 1–2 at amortized cost regardless of intent. CECL applies under GAAP only.
articles.key_difference: GAAP: classification-driven measurement. STAT: NAIC designation drives carrying value.
articles.gaap_view: ASC 326 (CECL) requires expected-loss provision on amortized-cost bonds. AFS bonds use OCI with credit-loss allowance through P&L.
articles.stat_view: SSAP 26R (corporate bonds) at amortized cost if NAIC 1–2 designation. SSAP 43R (RMBS/CMBS) uses modeling-based designation.
articles.body_md:
## Inventory

A typical US life insurer's bond book: Treasuries / Agencies 10–15%, Corporate IG 50–60%, Corporate HY 5–8%, Structured (CMBS, RMBS, CLO) 15–20%, Munis 5–10%.

## STAT designations & carrying value

- NAIC 1–2: amortized cost
- NAIC 3: amortized cost (with AVR provision)
- NAIC 4–5: lower of amortized cost or fair value
- NAIC 6: fair value

## Asset Valuation Reserve (AVR)

Life insurers post AVR — a contingency reserve absorbing realized and unrealized credit losses on the bond portfolio. AVR builds via formula component plus voluntary contribution and reduces surplus.

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content: GAAP requires positive intent + ability for HTM. AFS is the default for most insurer bond books. Trading is rare except for hedge-fund-style portfolios.

sections.heading: Impairment
sections.content: GAAP: CECL ECL allowance. STAT: write-down to fair value when 'other than temporarily impaired' under SSAP 43R modeling.

fsli_table.gaap: HTM amortized cost; CECL ECL allowance
fsli_table.delta: GAAP carries CECL allowance; STAT does not

fsli_table.stat: Lower of amortized cost or fair value
fsli_table.delta: STAT may carry below cost; AVR captures expected losses
GAAP and STAT designations can differ
NAIC has tightened CLO equity designations

articles.title: Equity Investments
articles.summary: Common, preferred, and partnership interests. GAAP measures all equities at fair value through P&L. STAT splits common (FV through surplus) from perpetual preferred (amortized cost if NAIC 1–2).
articles.key_difference: GAAP marks all equities to market through P&L. STAT routes most fair-value movements through surplus.
articles.gaap_view: ASC 321: fair value through net income. ASU 2016-01 eliminated AFS for equities.
articles.stat_view: SSAP 30 (common) at fair value, with unrealized through surplus. SSAP 32 (preferred): NAIC 1–2 at amortized cost.
articles.body_md:
## Why this matters

Post-ASU 2016-01, GAAP earnings are far more volatile for insurers with large equity portfolios. Berkshire Hathaway's quarterly net income now swings hundreds of billions on equity mark-to-market.

## Statutory smoothing

STAT routes equity unrealized gains directly through surplus. Statutory surplus is much less volatile than GAAP equity for the same portfolio.

sections.heading: Limited partnership accounting
items: Equity method when significant influence (>20%) under both GAAP and STAT.
STAT requires audited LP financials to recognize undistributed earnings.
Look-through to underlying assets is required for risk-based capital.

fsli_table.delta: GAAP P&L volatility vs STAT surplus volatility
STAT may exclude undistributed earnings without audit

articles.title: Commercial & Residential Mortgage Loans
articles.summary: Direct mortgage loans on income-producing properties. Life insurers hold ~10–20% of invested assets in CMLs. GAAP applies CECL; STAT uses SSAP 37 reserves and Schedule B reporting.
articles.key_difference: GAAP: CECL day-one. STAT: SSAP 37 mortgage-loan valuation reserve plus haircut for delinquent loans.
articles.gaap_view: ASC 310-20 amortized cost net of CECL allowance.
articles.stat_view: SSAP 37 — admitted at unpaid principal less mortgage-loan valuation reserve. Loans 90+ days delinquent are non-admitted unless adequately secured.
articles.body_md:
## Why insurers love CMLs

Commercial mortgage loans deliver duration-matched cash flows for long-tail liabilities, with ~50–100 bps of yield pickup over comparable corporate bonds.

## Underwriting filters

- LTV ≤ 65–70%
- Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) ≥ 1.30x
- Property types: office, multifamily, industrial, retail (selectively)

## CECL on CMLs (GAAP)

ASC 326-20 requires an expected-credit-loss allowance. Office CECL allowances surged 2023–2024 as work-from-home pressured CRE.

sections.heading: Risk-based capital
items: Life RBC for CMLs uses CM1 (best) through CM5 (worst).
Office in 2024 was placed under enhanced surveillance.
Mezzanine and B-piece loans treated separately under SSAP 37.

fsli_table.gaap: Same as senior with higher CECL
fsli_table.delta: RBC charge much higher under STAT

articles.title: Derivatives & Hedging (ASC 815)
articles.summary: Futures, forwards, swaps, options, and embedded derivatives. Used heavily by life insurers managing interest-rate, equity, and FX risk on annuity guarantees.
articles.key_difference: GAAP defaults to fair value through P&L with optional hedge accounting. STAT permits more hedge accounting flexibility.
articles.gaap_view: ASC 815: derivative at fair value through P&L. Hedge accounting reduces P&L volatility.
articles.stat_view: SSAP 86: replicates GAAP for non-hedging; hedge accounting available with simpler effectiveness tests.
articles.body_md:
## Insurer use cases

- Interest-rate swaps — duration-match annuity liabilities
- Currency swaps — hedge foreign bond exposure
- Equity total-return swaps / options — hedge variable-annuity GMxB benefits
- Inflation swaps — long-tail P&C liability hedging
- Credit default swaps — synthetic credit exposure

## Embedded derivatives

Variable-annuity guarantees (GMxB) often contain embedded derivatives that must be bifurcated under ASC 815-15. Post-LDTI, most market-risk benefits move to fair-value-through-P&L with non-performance risk in OCI.

sections.heading: MRBs vs embedded derivatives
sections.content: Pre-LDTI: GMAB/GMWB riders bifurcated as embedded derivatives. Post-LDTI: same riders measured as Market Risk Benefits at fair value with non-performance risk in OCI.

fsli_table.stat: Amortized cost when designated as hedge

fsli_table.line_item: Cash-flow hedge of forecasted bond purchase

fsli_table.gaap: FV through P&L (or part of MRB)

articles.title: Deferred Acquisition Costs (DAC)
articles.summary: Capitalized incremental, direct costs of acquiring insurance contracts. The single largest GAAP-vs-STAT divergence: GAAP capitalizes; STAT expenses immediately.
articles.key_difference: GAAP DAC asset → amortized over policy life. STAT: no DAC asset.
articles.gaap_view: ASC 944-30 (post-LDTI): capitalize incremental direct costs; amortize on a constant-level basis over expected contract term.
articles.stat_view: All acquisition costs expensed when incurred under SAP — no DAC asset.
articles.body_md:
## What qualifies for capitalization

Under ASC 944-30-25 (post-ASU 2018-12):

- First-year commissions ≥ ultimate renewal rate (incremental portion only)
- Underwriting expenses directly tied to successful issuance
- Medical exams, credit checks, contract-issuance costs

Non-incremental costs (general overhead, marketing without traceability) cannot be deferred.

## LDTI amortization

ASU 2018-12 swept away EGP-based amortization. Now: constant-level basis tied to a denominator (e.g. inforce face), no interest accrual, annual review prospective only.

## New-business strain

```
GAAP earnings on a new sale = First-year profit + DAC asset
STAT surplus impact = -(First-year acquisition costs)
```

A fast-growing life writer can show GAAP profits while burning statutory surplus.

sections.heading: Capitalization criteria
items: Incremental: would not have been incurred absent the contract.
Direct: traceable to contract acquisition.
Successful: only deferred for issued/booked contracts.

articles.title: Unpaid Claims & Loss Reserves (P&C)
articles.summary: P&C reserve for known and incurred-but-not-reported (IBNR) claims plus loss adjustment expense. Largest liability for P&C insurers; principal source of earnings volatility.
articles.key_difference: GAAP and STAT both undiscounted best estimate (with limited tabular exception); STAT adds appointed actuary opinion + Schedule P.
articles.gaap_view: ASC 944-40-30: best estimate of incurred-but-not-paid + IBNR + LAE, undiscounted.
articles.stat_view: SSAP 55 mirror; Schedule P discloses ten-accident-year loss development. Tabular discount permitted on workers' comp tabular indemnity.
articles.body_md:
## Components

```
Unpaid claims liability
  = Case reserves
  + Bulk reserves
  + IBNR
  + ALAE
  + ULAE
```

IBNR is computed actuarially using chain-ladder, Bornhuetter-Ferguson, expected-loss-ratio, or stochastic methods.

## Reserve adequacy & development

Favorable development: prior accident-year reserves released back through P&L. Adverse development: reserves strengthened, hitting current period.

## Loss ratio

```
Incurred losses = Paid losses + Δ Unpaid claims liability
Loss ratio = Incurred losses / Earned premium
```

sections.heading: Reserving methods
items: Chain-ladder — extrapolate paid/incurred development factors.
Bornhuetter-Ferguson — blends expected losses with actual emergence.
Expected loss ratio — apply prior-period loss ratios to current earned premium.
Stochastic — Mack, Bootstrap, Bayesian models.

sections.heading: Reserve adequacy review
sections.content: Quarterly under GAAP for SEC filers. STAT requires Statement of Actuarial Opinion at year-end signed by qualified appointed actuary.

fsli_table.stat: Included; reported separately on Schedule P

fsli_table.delta: STAT discount rate set by domiciliary state

articles.title: Liability for Future Policy Benefits (LDTI)
articles.summary: Reserve for long-duration insurance contracts. Reformed by ASU 2018-12 (LDTI), the largest GAAP insurance overhaul in 40 years.
articles.key_difference: GAAP post-LDTI: cohort-level LFPB with annual unlocking and current upper-medium-grade discount. STAT: principle-based reserves (PBR / VM-20) for life; CARVM for annuities.
articles.gaap_view: Annual review of cash-flow assumptions; retrospective unlocking through P&L. Discount rate updated each period.
articles.stat_view: VM-20 PBR uses prescribed mortality / lapse / yield assumptions and a deterministic + stochastic floor. CARVM (SSAP 51) for annuities.
articles.body_md:
## What LDTI changed

For SEC filers, LDTI (ASU 2018-12) became effective Jan 1, 2023:

1. Cohort-level LFPB
2. Annual unlocking with retrospective P&L impact
3. Discount rate: single-A-equivalent updated each period
4. Market Risk Benefits separately measured at fair value
5. DAC simplification — constant-level amortization

## The LFPB calculation

```
LFPB(t) = PV[future benefits] - PV[future net premiums]
        — measured at the cohort level, single-A discount rate
```

## Statutory contrast (PBR / CARVM)

Life insurers under VM-20 PBR compute reserves as the maximum of NPR, Deterministic Reserve, Stochastic Reserve.

sections.heading: Cohort definition
items: Issue year (calendar year of policy issuance).
Product / contract type.
Underwriting class.
Benefit feature.

fsli_table.stat: VM-20 PBR (max of NPR, DR, SR)
VM-20 PBR with mortality + lapse stress

fsli_table.delta: GAAP volatility from rates; STAT constant

fsli_table.gaap: Cohort LFPB; significant LTC re-measurement charges
fsli_table.stat: Active life / disabled life reserves under SSAP 54

articles.title: Market Risk Benefits (MRBs)
articles.summary: Separately measured reserve for variable-annuity guarantees (GMxB). Created by ASU 2018-12 to replace embedded-derivative bifurcation.
articles.key_difference: GAAP MRB at fair value with non-performance risk in OCI. STAT continues VM-21 methodology.
articles.gaap_view: Fair-value measurement; changes attributable to insurer's own credit (NPR) flow through OCI; remainder through P&L.
articles.stat_view: VM-21 reserves; stochastic CTE-70-based reserve under prescribed scenarios.
articles.body_md:
## What is an MRB?

A contractual feature that compels the insurer to make a payment based on a market event AND exposes the insurer to other-than-nominal capital-market risk.

Classic examples — variable-annuity rider guarantees: GMDB, GMAB, GMWB, GMIB.

## GAAP measurement

MRB liability = present value of expected guaranteed benefit payments over expected fees, computed under risk-neutral stochastic scenarios with the insurer's own credit spread.

## STAT (VM-21)

VM-21 calculates a stochastic reserve at CTE 70 under prescribed scenarios, with a clearly-defined hedging-credit framework.

fsli_table.gaap: MRB at fair value (P&L for market; OCI for own credit)

articles.title: Universal Life & Annuity Account Balances
articles.summary: Deposit-basis liability for universal-life and deferred-annuity contracts. Equals the policyholder's notional account balance plus any unearned-revenue liability.
articles.key_difference: GAAP and STAT both use deposit accounting; differences at the margins (DAC, secondary guarantees).
articles.gaap_view: Account balance + unearned-revenue liability for amortizable front loads.
articles.stat_view: Account balance under SSAP 51 + secondary-guarantee reserve under VM-20 if applicable.
articles.body_md:
## Mechanics

```
Account balance(t) = Account balance(t-1) + Premium paid - Withdrawals
                   - Cost-of-insurance charge - Expense load
                   + Interest credited
```

## Secondary guarantees

No-lapse universal-life (NLG) features promise the policy stays in force even if the account balance drops to zero. Secondary-guarantee reserves can be far larger than the account balance.

## Interest crediting

- UL: declared rate set by insurer, often with floor (3%, 2%, 1%, 0%)
- Indexed UL: cap/participation/floor on index linked to S&P 500
- Variable UL: separate-account performance flows directly to policyholder

articles.title: Premium Revenue Recognition
articles.summary: Earning of insurance premium across the policy coverage period. Short-duration earns ratably; long-duration earns when due; deposit contracts bypass premium revenue.
articles.key_difference: ASC 606 explicitly excludes insurance contracts. STAT mirrors GAAP with separate written-vs-earned tracking in Schedule P.
articles.gaap_view: Short-duration: pro-rata over coverage period. Long-duration: when due. Deposit contracts: no premium revenue.
articles.stat_view: Mirror of GAAP; written premium tracked separately for premium-deficiency and Schedule P loss-development analysis.
articles.body_md:
## Short-duration premium earning

A 12-month P&C policy with $1,200 annual premium written Jan 1:
- Written premium (Jan 1): $1,200
- Earned premium per month: $100
- Unearned premium (Jan 31): $1,100

## Long-duration premium earning

A whole-life policy: premium recognized as revenue when *due*, with the LFPB construct absorbing future benefits.

## Deposit accounting

For universal-life and deferred annuities, the entire premium is treated as a deposit — no premium revenue. Revenue comes from COI charges, expense loads, surrender charges, and investment-spread.

fsli_table.stat: Same; Schedule P tracks written and earned

articles.title: Premium Deficiency Reserve (PDR)
articles.summary: Recognized when expected future losses + LAE + maintenance costs exceed unearned premium reserve plus expected investment income.
articles.key_difference: Aligned trigger; STAT reports gross of reinsurance vs GAAP net.
articles.gaap_view: ASC 944-60-25: when PV of expected future costs exceeds UPR + DAC + investment income, recognize the shortfall.
articles.stat_view: SSAP 53 / SSAP 65 mirror; aggregation typically at line of business.
articles.body_md:
## Trigger formula

```
PDR = max(0,
  PV(future losses + LAE + maintenance) -
  Unearned premium reserve -
  DAC -
  Anticipated investment income on UPR cash flows
)
```

## DAC offset

When a deficiency exists, first write off DAC on the affected portfolio; if still deficient, recognize PDR.

## Examples

- Workers' comp 2009–2010: declining payroll exposures + medical inflation
- Long-term care 2017–2019: morbidity/lapse divergence triggered industry-wide PDRs

articles.title: Reinsurance Recoverables
articles.fsli: Reinsurance Recoverable on Paid & Unpaid Losses
articles.summary: Asset reflecting amounts due (paid) or expected (unpaid) from reinsurers. Separate asset on the balance sheet — never netted against gross liabilities.
articles.key_difference: GAAP requires CECL on reinsurance recoverables. STAT non-admits unauthorized + unsecured reinsurer recoverables.
articles.gaap_view: Recoverable at net realizable value with CECL allowance.
articles.stat_view: Admitted at expected amount; non-admitted to extent reinsurer is unauthorized + unsecured (SSAP 61R Schedule F).
articles.body_md:
## Why it's a separate asset

Reinsurance is treated as an indemnity contract — the cedent remains primarily liable. The reinsurer's promise creates an asset; the cedent's obligation remains a liability.

## CECL on reinsurance recoverables

Since Jan 2023, GAAP filers compute an expected-credit-loss allowance.

## Schedule F (STAT)

For each reinsurer, the cedent reports premium ceded, recoverables, authorized status, collateral, and slow-pay provision.

## Slow-pay provision

If a reinsurer is more than 90 days past-due, a 20% provision is recognized on the entire recoverable balance.

sections.heading: Collateral and credit
items: Letters of credit from rated banks reduce both GAAP CECL and STAT non-admission.
Funds withheld are functionally equivalent collateral.
Trust accounts (Section 114 trusts) common for unauthorized US reinsurers.

articles.title: Reinsurance Ceded — Prospective vs Retrospective
articles.summary: How a cedent recognizes premium and benefit when transferring risk. Bifurcation between prospective and retrospective is critical.
articles.key_difference: Largely aligned post-SSAP 62R Revisions.
articles.gaap_view: ASC 944-20-25-21: prospective recognized prospectively; retrospective requires deferral of any gain.
articles.stat_view: SSAP 62R mirrors GAAP for prospective; LPT/ADC accounting deposits any economic transfer not meeting risk-transfer test.
articles.body_md:
## Prospective reinsurance

Covers losses arising from events that occur **after** the contract effective date. Premium ceded recognized over coverage period.

## Retrospective reinsurance

Covers losses from events that occurred **before** the contract effective date — typically LPTs.

## Common contract types

- Quota share
- Excess of loss
- Stop loss
- Catastrophe XOL
- LPT (loss-portfolio transfer)
- ADC (adverse-development cover)

sections.heading: Funds-withheld accounting
sections.content: The cedent retains the premium asset and records a corresponding funds-withheld liability. Investment income belongs to the reinsurer.

articles.title: Risk Transfer Test (10/10 and beyond)
articles.summary: Test that determines whether a contract receives reinsurance accounting or deposit accounting.
articles.key_difference: Aligned post-2020.
articles.gaap_view: Significant insurance risk + reasonable possibility of significant loss → reinsurance accounting.
articles.stat_view: SSAP 62R Appendix A — risk-transfer assertions required; appointed actuary certification.
articles.body_md:
## Two prongs

**Prong 1 — Significant insurance risk**

The reinsurer must assume both timing and underwriting risk.

**Prong 2 — Reasonable possibility of significant loss**

Informal '10/10 rule': 10% probability of 10% economic loss.

## Failure modes

A reinsurance contract may fail when it has aggregate caps too low, profit-sharing reversing reinsurer losses, or experience-rating mechanisms returning gains to the cedent.

articles.title: Statutory Surplus & Risk-Based Capital
articles.summary: Statutory surplus = admitted assets - liabilities. RBC = formulaic calculation of required capital.
articles.key_difference: GAAP's analog is shareholders' equity. RBC is a uniquely statutory construct.
articles.gaap_view: Equity = total assets - total liabilities. No regulatory action levels.
articles.stat_view: Surplus = admitted assets - liabilities - AVR - IMR. RBC ratio = Total Adjusted Capital / Authorized Control Level RBC.
articles.body_md:
## RBC components (Life)

- C-0 Affiliate / off-balance-sheet risk
- C-1cs Stock asset risk
- C-1o Other asset risk (bonds, mortgages)
- C-2 Insurance risk (mortality, morbidity)
- C-3 Interest-rate risk
- C-4 Business risk

## Action levels

RBC ratio = TAC / ACL
- ≥ 200% — No action
- 150-200% — Company action
- 100-150% — Regulatory action
- 70-100% — Authorized control
- < 70% — Mandatory control

## AVR and IMR (Life)

- Asset Valuation Reserve — contingency reserve absorbing credit losses
- Interest Maintenance Reserve — defers rate-driven realized gains on bonds

articles.title: Current Expected Credit Losses (CECL)
articles.summary: ASU 2016-13's expected-credit-loss model replaced the incurred-loss approach for most financial instruments.
articles.key_difference: STAT does not adopt CECL.
articles.gaap_view: Day-one expected credit loss allowance covering the contractual life.
articles.stat_view: Bonds: SSAP 26R/43R OTTI write-downs. Receivables: non-admission rules.
articles.body_md:
## What CECL covers

1. HTM bonds (ASC 326-20) — full lifetime ECL
2. AFS bonds (ASC 326-30) — only when FV < AC AND credit deterioration
3. Mortgage loans
4. Reinsurance recoverables
5. Premium receivables
6. Loan commitments and standby letters of credit

## Methods

- Vintage analysis
- Probability-weighted scenarios
- Discounted cash flow
- WARM (weighted-average remaining maturity)

articles.summary: Top-level US GAAP standard governing insurance accounting.

articles.stat_view: Conservative, liquidity/solvency-focused.

articles.title: LDTI (ASU 2018-12) — Long-Duration Reform
articles.summary: Most significant US GAAP insurance change in decades. Effective 2023 for SEC filers.
articles.key_difference: Annual unlocking, cohort-level LFPB, MRBs at fair value, constant-level DAC.
articles.gaap_view: Cohort-level LFPB with annual review; MRBs at fair value; DAC simplified.
articles.stat_view: VM-20 PBR + CARVM continue.
articles.body_md:
## Five major changes

1. LFPB cohorts
2. Annual unlocking with retrospective P&L impact
3. Discount rate updated each period
4. MRBs separately measured at fair value
5. DAC simplified to constant-level amortization

## Industry impact

- Heavy implementation costs ($50M–$200M per major insurer)
- Earnings volatility increased materially
- LTC unlockings 2023–2024: $200M–$2B per insurer

articles.title: FAS 60 — Short-Duration Contracts (legacy)
articles.summary: Original P&C accounting model. Premium earned ratably over coverage; losses recognized as incurred.
articles.key_difference: Aligned to STAT for most short-duration items.
articles.gaap_view: Pro-rata premium earning; undiscounted loss reserves; DAC asset; premium-deficiency test.
articles.stat_view: Same earning pattern; Schedule P loss-development triangles required.
articles.body_md:
## Snapshot

**Scope.** Most P&C policies and short-duration health.

**Premium recognition.** Earned ratably over the coverage period.

**Loss reserves.** Best estimate of unpaid claims (case + IBNR), undiscounted.

**DAC.** Capitalized; amortized in proportion to premium revenue.

## Key disclosures

ASU 2015-09 added disclosures: paid loss triangle, incurred loss triangle, claim count triangle for the most recent ten accident years.

articles.title: FAS 97 — Universal Life & Investment Contracts (legacy)
articles.summary: Established account-balance (deposit) accounting for universal life and deferred annuities.
articles.key_difference: Aligned with STAT account-balance treatment; major divergence at DAC and secondary-guarantee reserves.
articles.gaap_view: Account balance + unearned-revenue liability for front loads.
articles.stat_view: Account balance under SSAP 51; secondary-guarantee reserve under VM-20.
articles.body_md: Snapshot — see Universal Life article for full FSLI-level detail.

articles.title: FAS 133 — Derivatives & Hedging (legacy)
articles.summary: Original derivative-and-hedging standard. Modernized into ASC 815 with ASU 2017-12 simplifications.
articles.key_difference: Aligned to ASC 815 article.
articles.gaap_view: Fair value + hedge designation framework.
articles.stat_view: SSAP 86 — more flexible hedge accounting.
articles.body_md: See ASC 815 article for full derivatives & hedging detail.

articles.title: Statutory Accounting Principles (SAP)
articles.summary: Regulator-driven framework focused on solvency and policyholder protection.
articles.key_difference: Conservative, liquidation-oriented vs going-concern GAAP.
articles.gaap_view: Going-concern, asset-rich, deferred-cost emphasis.
articles.stat_view: Liquidation-basis, conservative reserves, non-admitted assets, RBC-driven.
articles.body_md:
## Why two sets of books?

U.S. insurers prepare both **GAAP** (for investors) and **STAT** (for regulators) financials. Statutory accounting is intentionally conservative — it answers *can the company pay claims if it stopped writing tomorrow?*

## Key SAP traits

- Non-admitted assets (DAC, furniture, prepaid) excluded from surplus
- DAC is **expensed** when incurred
- Investments at amortized cost for high-quality bonds
- Dividends require regulatory approval if exceeding ordinary thresholds

## Statutory schedules

- A — Real estate
- B — Mortgage loans
- BA — Other long-term invested assets
- D — Bonds and stocks
- DA — Short-term investments
- DB — Derivatives
- E — Cash & equivalents
- F — Reinsurance
- P — Loss development triangles
- SI — Permitted/prescribed practices
- T — Premium by state

articles.title: Combined Ratio — The P&C Scoreboard
articles.summary: Combined Ratio = Loss Ratio + Expense Ratio. Below 100% means underwriting profit; above 100% means underwriting loss.
articles.key_difference: GAAP uses earned premium in expense-ratio denominator; STAT uses written premium.
articles.gaap_view: Earned-premium denominator across both ratios.
articles.stat_view: Written-premium denominator for expense ratio.
articles.body_md:
## Formula

```
Loss Ratio       = Incurred Losses & LAE / Earned Premium
Expense Ratio    = Underwriting Expenses / Earned Premium  (GAAP)
                 = Underwriting Expenses / Written Premium (STAT)
Combined Ratio   = Loss Ratio + Expense Ratio
```

## Reading it

- < 95%   = strong underwriting
- 95-100% = profitable
- 100-105% = breakeven; relying on investment income
- > 105%  = underwriting loss

articles.title: Schedule P — Loss Development
articles.summary: Triangle of paid and incurred losses by accident year for the most recent 10 years.
articles.key_difference: STAT-only schedule, mirrored in part by GAAP's ASU 2015-09 development triangles.
articles.gaap_view: ASU 2015-09 disclosure for SEC filers.
articles.stat_view: Schedule P parts 1-7 detail each line of business.
articles.body_md:
## Parts of Schedule P

- Part 1 — Loss summary by line
- Part 2 — Incurred losses & ALAE (triangle)
- Part 3 — Cumulative paid losses & ALAE (triangle)
- Part 4 — Bulk + IBNR (triangle)
- Part 5 — Claim counts (triangle)
- Part 6 — Premium history
- Part 7 — Reinsurance

articles.title: Schedule F — Reinsurance
articles.summary: By-reinsurer ledger of premium ceded, recoverables, collateral, authorized status, and slow-pay provisions.
articles.key_difference: STAT-only schedule.
articles.gaap_view: Concentration disclosure required under ASC 944-310.
articles.stat_view: Schedule F Parts 1-9 provide reinsurer-level detail.
articles.body_md:
## Parts of Schedule F

- Part 1 — Premium ceded
- Part 2 — Premium assumed
- Part 3 — Recoverable on paid losses
- Part 4 — Recoverable on unpaid losses
- Part 5 — Reinsurance collateral analysis
- Part 6 — Authorized vs unauthorized + slow-pay calculation
- Part 7 — Restatement of prior year amounts
- Part 8 — Reinsurance treaty terms
- Part 9 — Captive reinsurance

articles.title: Income Taxes for Insurers (ASC 740)
articles.summary: Insurers operate with substantial DTAs from loss reserves, DAC tax-deferral, and net operating losses.
articles.key_difference: GAAP recognizes all DTAs net of valuation allowance. STAT admits DTAs subject to a three-bucket test.
articles.gaap_view: Recognize DTAs at enacted rates; reduce by valuation allowance when realization is not more-likely-than-not.
articles.stat_view: SSAP 101: admitted DTA = sum of three buckets; excess non-admitted.
articles.body_md:
## Insurer-specific DTA sources

- Loss-reserve discount under §846
- DAC §848 — proxy DAC amortization for tax
- Long-tail loss reserves generate large temporary differences
- NOL carryforwards (post-2017 TCJA: 80% offset)

## SSAP 101 admitted DTA

1. Bucket 1: Federal income taxes recoverable from prior years
2. Bucket 2: DTAs reversing within 1-3 years
3. Bucket 3: DTAs offsetting DTLs of the same character

articles.title: Policyholder Dividends
articles.summary: Distributions to participating-policy holders. Mutual-life insurers typically declare a substantial annual policyholder dividend.
articles.key_difference: Aligned: liability accrues over the policy year and is recognized as expense.
articles.gaap_view: ASC 944-50: accrue dividend over the policy year.
articles.stat_view: SSAP 65 mirror — dividends declared from divisible surplus.
articles.body_md:
## Mutual companies

Northwestern Mutual, MassMutual, New York Life distribute hundreds of millions to billions in annual policyholder dividends — driven by favorable mortality, investment yield above credited rate, and expense savings.

articles.title: Business Combinations — Insurer Specifics (VOBA)
articles.summary: Insurance M&A creates Value of Business Acquired (VOBA) — present value of future profits embedded in acquired contracts.
articles.key_difference: GAAP fully recognizes VOBA. STAT generally writes off target's DAC; goodwill admission severely limited.
articles.gaap_view: Identify and value VOBA at fair value; amortize on a basis consistent with original DAC method.
articles.stat_view: SSAP 68 limits goodwill admission to 10% of subsidiary capital; amortized over 10 years.
articles.body_md:
## VOBA mechanics

At the acquisition date:

1. Determine fair value of acquired contracts using actuarial appraisal
2. Recognize VOBA at this fair value
3. Amortize over expected contract term
4. The target's pre-existing DAC is written off

## STAT goodwill

- Recognized goodwill = excess of investment in subsidiary over its statutory equity
- Admitted only to lesser of 10% of acquirer's capital, OR amortizable amount
- Amortized over not more than 10 years

articles.title: Embedded Derivatives in Variable Annuities (ASC 815-15)
articles.summary: Bifurcation of variable-annuity guarantees as embedded derivatives. Largely superseded for GMxB by LDTI MRBs but still applicable to indexed-annuity participation, GMIB-style benefits not in MRB scope, and stable-value features.
articles.key_difference: GAAP requires explicit bifurcation when the embedded feature is not clearly and closely related to the host. STAT (SSAP 86) follows the same logic with surplus-rather-than-P&L volatility.
articles.gaap_view: Bifurcate; measure embedded at fair value through P&L. Host contract continues at amortized / deposit basis.
articles.stat_view: Bifurcate per SSAP 86; embedded at fair value through surplus.
articles.body_md:
## When to bifurcate

Three-prong test (ASC 815-15-25-1):
1. The embedded feature meets the definition of a derivative.
2. The embedded is **not** clearly and closely related to the host.
3. A separate freestanding instrument with the same terms would be a derivative.

## Indexed-annuity participation

For an equity-indexed annuity, the index-credit feature is bifurcated as an embedded derivative because the equity-linked return is not clearly and closely related to the fixed-rate host contract.

## GMIB and stable-value

GMIB benefits with restrictive annuitization conditions can fall outside the MRB scope and remain bifurcated as embedded derivatives. Stable-value wraps over separate-account portfolios are typically embedded derivatives.

## Risk transfer (LPT) interaction

If an insurer cedes a contract with embedded derivatives via reinsurance, the assumed contract is re-evaluated for bifurcation at the reinsurer level — same test, same result.

sections.heading: Clearly-and-closely-related test
items: Equity-linked features in fixed contracts → not clearly and closely related → bifurcate.
Inflation-linked features in fixed contracts → typically clearly and closely related → no bifurcation.
Currency-linked features → almost always bifurcate.

fsli_table.gaap: Embedded derivative when wrap protects unit value at FV
Now an MRB, not embedded derivative

articles.title: Segment Reporting for Insurers (ASC 280)
articles.summary: Insurers typically present segments by line of business (P&C, Life, Health, Reinsurance) and within those by geography or distribution channel. Updated by ASU 2023-07 to require Significant Segment Expense disclosures.
articles.key_difference: STAT does not require segment reporting; the analog is the Statutory Annual Statement Schedule T (premium by state) and line-of-business detail in P&E pages.
articles.gaap_view: ASC 280 management approach: segments mirror how the CODM reviews performance. ASU 2023-07 (effective 2024) requires disclosure of significant segment expenses regularly reviewed.
articles.stat_view: No formal segments; line-of-business reporting baked into the Annual Statement.
articles.body_md:
## Management approach

Segments must mirror how the chief operating decision maker (CODM) reviews and allocates resources — not necessarily legal entity or product structure.

## Insurer disclosures

- Premium by segment (gross, ceded, net)
- Combined ratio by segment
- Capital allocated by segment (often disclosed)
- Investment income allocation

## ASU 2023-07

New requirement: disclose **significant segment expenses** that are regularly reviewed by the CODM. Effective 2024 for SEC filers. Insurers historically aggregated; now they must disaggregate (e.g. underwriting expense, claims expense, commissions).

articles.title: Leases for Insurers (ASC 842)
articles.summary: Insurers capitalize all operating leases on the balance sheet under ASC 842 (effective 2019). STAT under SSAP 22R retains operating-lease expense recognition without ROU asset.
articles.key_difference: GAAP recognizes ROU asset + lease liability for both operating and finance leases. STAT continues operating-lease expensing — no balance-sheet asset.
articles.gaap_view: Recognize ROU asset and lease liability at PV of remaining payments. Operating lease: straight-line expense. Finance lease: interest + amortization.
articles.stat_view: SSAP 22R: operating-lease expense recognized as paid; finance lease capitalized similar to GAAP. ROU asset for operating leases is non-admitted.
articles.body_md:
## ROU asset for insurers

Insurer real-estate footprint (HQ, branch network, claims-adjustment offices) can run into hundreds of millions in ROU assets — meaningful balance-sheet line for the largest carriers.

## STAT non-admission

The ROU asset for an operating lease is non-admitted under SAP, reducing surplus. Many insurers separately disclose the GAAP ROU + lease-liability impact in the GAAP-to-STAT reconciliation.

articles.title: ORSA — Own Risk and Solvency Assessment
articles.summary: Annual self-assessment by US insurers of their material risks and capital adequacy under multiple stress scenarios. Required by all NAIC member states for insurers above the premium threshold.
articles.key_difference: ORSA is a STAT-only construct; no GAAP analog. Reported confidentially to the lead state.
articles.gaap_view: No equivalent. Some elements appear in MD&A risk disclosure and 10-K Item 7A market-risk quantitative disclosure.
articles.stat_view: Annual ORSA Summary Report covering Risk Management Framework, Risk Profile, and Group Capital Assessment.
articles.body_md:
## Three sections of an ORSA report

1. **Risk-Management Framework** — governance, risk appetite, risk identification.
2. **Risk Profile** — material risks: insurance, market, credit, liquidity, operational, strategic, reputation.
3. **Group Solvency Assessment** — projected capital under base + stress scenarios over a multi-year horizon.

## Threshold

US insurance groups with > $1B in annual premiums must file ORSA annually with their lead state regulator. Group Capital Calculation (GCC) and Liquidity Stress Test (LST) are companion exercises.

## Stress scenarios

Typical ORSA stress scenarios:
- 2008-style market crash
- 1-in-200 catastrophe
- Pandemic shock
- Combined adverse market + insurance scenario

sections.heading: Reporting calendar
items: Q4 each calendar year — board-approved final report.
Confidential filing with lead state.
Coordinated with the international group capital aggregator (US has GCC; international has ICS).

fsli_table.stat: Annual filing required by NAIC ORSA Model Act
Companion to ORSA; aggregates capital across the group

articles.title: IFRS 17 vs US GAAP — Comparison
articles.summary: IFRS 17 (effective Jan 2023) replaced IFRS 4 with three measurement models: General Measurement Model (GMM), Premium Allocation Approach (PAA), Variable Fee Approach (VFA). Significant differences from US GAAP LDTI persist.
articles.key_difference: IFRS 17 introduces the Contractual Service Margin (CSM) — unearned profit released as services are provided. US GAAP under LDTI keeps separate revenue and benefit-recognition mechanics with no equivalent CSM.
articles.gaap_view: ASC 944 LDTI: net-premium ratio approach; LFPB at single-A discount.
articles.stat_view: Not applicable — IFRS not used by US-domiciled insurers for regulatory reporting.
articles.body_md:
## IFRS 17's three models

| Model | When applied | Key feature |
|---|---|---|
| GMM | Long-duration, no direct participation | Build-up of CSM for unearned profit |
| PAA | Short-duration ≤ 12m | Simplified; analog to FAS 60 / ASC 944 short-duration |
| VFA | Direct-participation contracts (UL, VA with significant link) | CSM adjusted for share of underlying-item changes |

## CSM (Contractual Service Margin)

The CSM represents unearned profit at issue, released as the insurer provides services over the contract life. Under IFRS 17, gain on day-one is impossible; any expected loss is recognized immediately.

## Discount rate

- IFRS 17: current rate updated each reporting period; can use top-down or bottom-up.
- US GAAP LDTI: current upper-medium-grade (single-A) yield.

## Why this matters for global insurers

US-listed groups with international subsidiaries (AIG, MetLife, Manulife/MFC) must reconcile US GAAP and IFRS 17, often with multi-billion-dollar impact differences.

fsli_table.delta: IFRS 17 GMM with CSM separates unearned profit explicitly

articles.title: NAIC Climate Risk Disclosure & Climate Scenario Analysis
articles.summary: Annual NAIC survey aligned with TCFD (Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures). Mandatory for insurers above the premium threshold in 15+ participating states.
articles.key_difference: STAT-driven survey; SEC has separate climate disclosure rule (currently in litigation).
articles.gaap_view: 10-K Item 1A risk factors typically include climate; SEC's separate climate disclosure rule (2024) added more rigor.
articles.stat_view: NAIC Climate Risk Disclosure Survey — public, four sections: governance, strategy, risk management, metrics & targets.
articles.body_md:
## TCFD alignment

The NAIC survey since 2022 mirrors the TCFD framework:

1. **Governance** — board oversight of climate risks
2. **Strategy** — how climate scenarios shape underwriting / investment
3. **Risk Management** — identification, assessment, integration
4. **Metrics & Targets** — Scope 1/2/3 emissions, transition / physical risk metrics

## SEC climate rule (March 2024)

Requires registered companies (including insurers) to disclose climate-related risks, governance, and Scope 1/2 GHG emissions. Currently stayed pending litigation.

## Insurer-specific concerns

- Property-cat exposure to physical risk
- Investment-portfolio transition risk (fossil-fuel issuers)
- Liability-side reserve impacts on long-tail health (climate-sensitive disease)

fsli_table.delta: Both required for largest US insurers

articles.title: Captive Insurance
articles.framework: NAIC Captive Insurance Model Act / Domiciliary State Statutes
articles.summary: A wholly-owned subsidiary insuring the risks of its parent. Used for risk financing, tax efficiency, and access to reinsurance markets. Common domiciles: Vermont, Bermuda, Cayman, South Carolina.
articles.key_difference: Captives are statutory entities subject to SAP, but typically with relaxed capital requirements vs commercial carriers in their domicile.
articles.gaap_view: Consolidation per ASC 810; eliminate intercompany premium and reserves. Risk transfer must still be assessed (ASC 944-20-15-41).
articles.stat_view: Domiciliary regulator dictates capital, reserves, and reporting. Many domiciles allow letter-of-credit-funded captive surplus.
articles.body_md:
## Common captive structures

- **Single-parent captive** — subsidiary writing only the parent's risks
- **Group captive** — multiple unrelated parents share a captive
- **Cell captive (PCC)** — protected-cell structure with segregated risk pools
- **Risk Retention Group (RRG)** — federal vehicle for liability-only group captives

## Insurance-industry use cases

- Life insurers reinsuring older blocks to a captive (XXX/AXXX captive structures pre-2014)
- P&C insurers retaining workers' comp self-insurance via captive
- Captives writing layer of catastrophe attachment

## Risk-transfer scrutiny

IRS and SEC scrutinize captives for risk-transfer adequacy. Failed risk transfer makes the contract a deposit — eliminating any tax-deduction benefit and forcing different financial-reporting treatment.

## Regulatory landscape

- NAIC AG 48 (2014) clamped down on XXX/AXXX captives
- IRS §831(b) micro-captives: heightened audit risk
- US-domiciled captives reporting SAP financials to home state

fsli_table.stat: Recorded by both cedent and captive entity
fsli_table.delta: GAAP consolidates away; STAT keeps both sides

articles.title: IRS §846 — Loss Reserve Tax Discount
articles.summary: Federal tax rules require P&C insurers to discount their loss reserves for tax purposes. Creates a permanent gap between book (undiscounted) reserves and tax (discounted) reserves — drives substantial DTAs.
articles.key_difference: Tax-only construct. GAAP and STAT loss reserves are undiscounted; the tax-discounting requirement creates large temporary differences.
articles.gaap_view: Undiscounted on balance sheet; deferred tax asset recognized for the discount difference.
articles.stat_view: Same — undiscounted; SSAP 101 governs DTA admission of the timing difference.
articles.body_md:
## How discounting works for tax

The IRS publishes annual loss-payment patterns and discount factors by line of business under Rev. Proc. issuances. Insurers apply the discount factor to undiscounted loss reserves to arrive at tax-deductible reserves.

## TCJA 2017 changes

- Discount rate: corporate-bond yield curve (replaced midterm AFR)
- Loss patterns: industry-wide rather than company-specific
- Phase-in over 8 years for transitional difference

## Insurer impact

Workers' comp, medical malpractice, products liability — long-tail lines — generate the largest tax-discount differences. DTAs from these timing differences can run to billions for the largest carriers.
